transcend

tran-SEND · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To transcend is to go beyond the range or limits of something; to rise above it entirely.

The old folk song transcends language, moving audiences to tears whether or not they understand the words.

Example

Great art, the critic argued, transcends the era in which it was made, speaking just as powerfully to audiences a hundred years later.

To transcend something is to go beyond its usual limits entirely -- rising above boundaries like language, time, or category.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

surpass: To surpass is to do better than a rival or a benchmark on the same scale — you surpass a record, a rival, an expectation. To transcend is to leave the scale itself behind, rising out of a category's limits altogether.

exceed: To exceed is to go past a set, measurable limit — a budget, a speed limit, a quota. Transcend is larger and less numerical: rising above a whole boundary such as language, time, or category, not just overshooting a figure.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fall short: to fail to reach a standard or expectation

limit: to restrict the extent or amount of something

Where it sits · how far beyond the boundary it goes

cross → transcend → revolutionize

cross vs. transcend: To cross a boundary is far weaker than to transcend it: crossing is plain movement over a line, while transcending means rising above the boundary's limits entirely.

revolutionize vs. transcend: To revolutionize something goes even further than transcending it, completely transforming it into something new.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — trans-: across, beyond (Latin trans, 'across')

root — -scend: to climb (Latin scandere, 'to climb')

Put it together: Transcend combines trans- ('across, beyond') with scandere ('to climb') -- literally 'to climb beyond,' rising above the usual limits of something.

Use the root in a new word: ascend: The climbing team radioed that they would descend before the storm closed in.

Root Check

Word Choice

Transcend often appears with abstract limits -- language, time, culture, expectations -- rather than physical objects. (An earlier morpheme unit in this course taught condescend, which shares this same Latin root but means something quite different: to act as if you're above someone, in a negative sense.)
